text: When Gorgias became governor of Idumea,<sup>[99]</sup> he hired an army of professional soldiers and attacked our people whenever he could.
comment: [99] Idumea: The Greek has “the region.” According to 12.32 the region is Idumea, an area just south of Judea and the home of the Herod family mentioned frequently in the New Testament.

text: Even the Idumeans themselves attacked us, hoping to turn the whole country into a battleground.<sup>[100]</sup> They controlled strong fortresses and welcomed all the troublemakers who had been run out of Jerusalem.
comment: [100] hoping to turn … battleground: Or “hoping to make the war last as long as possible.”

text: Because of these attacks, Judas and his troops begged God for help. Then they quickly set out for the Idumean fortresses.

They made violent attacks on them and forced the enemy soldiers to retreat from their positions on the walls. Then after they had captured these places, they killed everyone they could. At least 20,000 of their enemies died.
About 9,000 enemy troops took cover in two strong towers that had everything they needed to fight off attackers.

So Judas ordered his brothers Simon and Joseph, along with an officer named Zacchaeus and his troops, to surround these towers. And since they had enough soldiers to capture the towers, Judas left for other parts of the country that needed his help even more.
But a few of Simon's troops became greedy. They took a bribe of 12,000 silver coins from some enemy forces in the towers, then let them sneak away.

When Judas found out what had happened, he called together his officers and brought charges against these soldiers. He said, “They have sold out their friends, and now the enemy troops who escaped will return and attack us.”
Judas had the guilty soldiers put to death. Then he and his troops immediately captured the two towers
and killed more than 20,000 enemy soldiers. Judas was successful in every battle he fought.

Someone named Timothy got together a powerful force of foreign soldiers, as well as a large number of cavalry from Asia. He then set out to invade Judea, even though he had already been defeated once before<sup>[101]</sup> by the Jewish troops.
comment: [101] even though … before: Or “even though another commander named Timothy had already been defeated.”

text: As Timothy's army came nearer, Judas and our troops prayed sincerely. They smeared dirt on their heads and put on clothes made of sackcloth.<sup>[102]</sup>
<sup>ⓙ</sup> Then they lay face down on the steps leading to the altar and prayed, “Please be kind to us and wipe out our enemies, just as our sacred Scriptures promise.”
After Judas and his troops had finished praying, they picked up their weapons and set out from Jerusalem on a long march. They camped not far from the enemy army,
and at dawn the next day the battle began. Our troops were brave and they trusted the Lord, which was a sure path to victory. But Timothy's soldiers fought only because they were angry.
In the heat of battle, the enemy saw five handsome riders on horses with gold bridles suddenly appear from heaven and take command of our troops.

They formed a circle around Judas and protected him with their shields and weapons, while sending a flood of arrows and lightning bolts at Timothy's army. Blinded and confused, the enemy troops scattered in every direction and were cut down.
Twenty thousand five hundred of their soldiers and 600 of their cavalry died that day.
Timothy himself escaped to the fortress at Gazara, where his brother Chaereas<sup>[103]</sup> commanded a large force.
Judas and his troops eagerly attacked Gazara for four days.
But the enemy soldiers inside the fortress kept cursing God and shouting horrible insults, because they felt safe behind the strong walls of their fortress.
Finally these insults made 20 of our brave young soldiers furious. So at dawn of the fifth day, they fought their way over the fortress wall, killing everyone they met.

At the same time, others fought their way over another section of the wall and attacked. They set fire to the whole fortress, including its towers, and burned alive those troops who had cursed God. Then some of our soldiers beat down the gates, allowing the rest of our army to capture the town.
Timothy was found hiding in a cistern, and so our troops killed him, together with his brother Chaereas and a soldier named Apollophanes.
After the battle, Judas and our army sang hymns of praise to the Lord, because he is very kind to Israel and gives us victory.

Lysias was a relative and the guardian of young King Antiochus Eupator.<sup>[104]</sup> He was also running the government for the king. Soon afterwards, when Lysias learned what had happened to Timothy, he became furious
comment: [104] young King Antiochus Eupator: Antiochus V; see the note at 2.19-23. He was only about nine years old when he became king.

text: and got together his cavalry and almost 80,000 soldiers to attack our people. He planned to turn Jerusalem into a Greek city
and to tax the temple, as he had done to the temples in other nations. He also wanted to sell the position of high priest to the highest bidder each year.
Lysias took great pride in his army that had tens of thousands of soldiers, as well as thousands of cavalry troops and 80 elephants. But he completely forgot about the power of God.
Lysias led this army into Judea, where he fiercely attacked the fortress at Beth-Zur, about 32 kilometers from Jerusalem.
Meanwhile, Judas and his soldiers found out that Lysias was attacking the fortresses. So they and everyone else cried and begged God to send a good angel to rescue Israel.

When they had finished praying, Judas was the first to reach for his weapons. Then he urged his troops to do the same. “Let's save our people, no matter what the cost!” he said. They eagerly set out for the enemy camp.
But no sooner had they left Jerusalem, than they noticed someone on horseback leading them. He was dressed in white and carrying weapons of gold.
Together they thanked God for having pity on them and sending an angel. They felt brave enough to attack humans, or the most savage animals, or even fortresses of solid iron.
Our troops marched in battle formation, led by the angel that their merciful Lord had sent.
They attacked the enemy army like lions, killing 11,000 soldiers and 1,600 cavalry. The rest of the enemy soldiers ran for their lives,
since most of them were wounded and without weapons. Lysias himself ran away like a coward.

Lysias was a smart man, and he kept thinking about the defeat he had just suffered. Finally, he realized he could never destroy the Jewish people. After all, God All-Powerful fought on our side. So he wrote a letter
urging our people to sign a peace treaty that would be fair. Lysias also promised that he would persuade King Antiochus to be kind to our nation.<sup>[105]</sup>
comment: [105] Lysias … nation: One possible meaning for the difficult Greek text.

text: Judas wanted to do what was best for everyone, so he agreed to do what Lysias had asked, since the king had always agreed to every request that he had made in writing to Lysias.<sup>[106]</sup>
comment: [106] since … Lysias: One possible meaning for the difficult Greek text.

text: This is a copy of the letter that Lysias wrote: Lysias sends greetings to the Jewish people.
You sent your messengers John and Absalom to me with your official list of demands, and we have gone over them in detail.
Some of the items on the list needed to be discussed with the king. So I did this, and he has agreed to do all he possibly can.
Meanwhile, remain faithful to our government, and from now on I'll do everything I can to make your nation prosper.
I have ordered John and Absalom, together with my own messengers, to discuss the details of this matter with you.
Goodbye. The date of this letter is the twenty-fourth day of the month of Dioscorinthius<sup>[107]</sup> in the year 148<sup>[108]</sup> of the Syrian Kingdom.
This is a copy of the letter that Antiochus wrote to Lysias: King Antiochus sends greetings to his good friend<sup>[109]</sup> Lysias.
comment: [109] good friend: See the note at 1.13,14.

text: Now that my father is dead, I am letting everyone in my kingdom take charge of their own lives, without being bothered by anyone.
I know the Jews refused to obey my father, who wanted them to live like Greeks. But they have their own customs and have asked permission to live according to their laws.
I have decided the Jews are free to live the way they want, just like any other nation in my kingdom. So give them back their temple and let them follow the traditions of their ancestors.
Send messengers to inform the Jews of my decision and to guarantee them that we are now on good terms. They will be glad to know that they can live in peace and do as they wish.
This is a copy of the letter from Antiochus to our nation: King Antiochus sends greetings to the Jews and their council.
I am in good health, and I hope you are too.
Menelaus the high priest<sup>[110]</sup> told me that you want to return home and live according to your traditions.
I will let you do that, but you must leave by the thirtieth day of the month Xanthicus<sup>[111]</sup> if you want to stay on good terms with me.
comment: [111] Xanthicus: A month from the Macedonian calendar; possibly Nisan or Adar of the Jewish calendar.

text: I also give you permission to continue your food laws and other customs. None of you will be punished for what you have done in ignorance.
I have sent Menelaus to encourage you.
Goodbye. The date of this letter is the fifteenth day of the month of Xanthicus in the year 148<sup>[112]</sup> of the Syrian Kingdom.
This is a copy of the letter the Romans sent to the Jews: Quintus Memmius and Titus Manius, messengers from Rome, send greetings to the Jews.
Rome approves the terms of the peace treaty that you were given by Lysias, the relative of King Antiochus.

We are now on the way to the city of Antioch, and we want you to study carefully the matters that Lysias discussed with the king. Then quickly send a messenger to us, and we will inform the king what is in your best interests.
Do not delay. Send the messengers as soon as you can, because we need to know how you feel about these matters.
Goodbye. The date of this letter is the fifteenth day of the month of Xanthicus<sup>[113]</sup> in the year 148<sup>[114]</sup> of the Syrian Kingdom.
comment:
[114] year 148: That is, 164 B.C.
[113] Xanthicus: See the note at 11.30.

text: After the agreement was signed, Lysias went back to King Antiochus, and our people started farming again.
But some of the local officials, especially Timothy, Apollonius,<sup>[115]</sup> Hieronymus, and Demophon, kept causing trouble, and so did Nicanor, who was an official in Cyprus.

The people of Joppa also committed a terrible crime against their Jewish neighbors. They pretended to be on good terms with them and said, “We want you and your families to go sailing with us. We'll provide the ships.”

They accepted this invitation since the whole town of Joppa had voted to invite them. Besides, they wanted to be on good terms with the Gentiles and didn't suspect a plot. But when the ships reached the open sea, the people of Joppa drowned about 200 of the Jews.
When Judas heard that such cruel things had been done to his own people, he told his troops what had to be done.<sup>[116]</sup>
comment: [116] he told … to be done: Or “he got his soldiers together.”

text: Everyone prayed to God, who always judges fairly. Then after dark, Judas and his troops attacked the murderers and set the harbor on fire. They destroyed its ships and killed everyone they caught hiding there.
But when Judas found the gates to Joppa closed, he led his troops away, planning to wipe out the town another time.
Judas was then told that the citizens of Jamnia also planned to kill their Jewish neighbors.
So one night, he and his troops attacked the town and set fire to the harbor and its ships. The light from the fire could be seen 45 kilometers away in Jerusalem.
Judas and his troops left Jamnia to go after Timothy.<sup>[117]</sup> But about a kilometer and a half from town, they were attacked by a force of almost 5,000 Arabs and 500 cavalry.
The fighting was fierce. But God helped Judas defeat these desert tribes, and they begged Judas for peace and offered him cattle and promised other help as well.
Judas knew they could be useful in many ways, and so he agreed to make peace. The Arabs accepted his terms and went back to their camp.
Then Judas surrounded the fortress at Caspin, a town protected by huge mounds of earth<sup>[118]</sup> and high walls. Foreigners from many places lived there,
comment: [118] huge mounds of earth: One possible meaning for the difficult Greek text.

text: and they had a large supply of food. In fact, they felt so secure behind their walls that they shouted insults against Judas and his troops, and they cursed God.

Judas and his troops prayed, “Lord God All-Powerful, you rule the world. And long ago, when Joshua was our leader, you helped our people destroy the town of Jericho, without using anything to knock down the gates or climb over the walls.” Then our troops fiercely attacked Caspin,
because God wanted them to capture it. They killed countless enemies—so many that a nearby lake, which was 370 meters wide, seemed to be filled with blood.
From Caspin, Judas led his troops 137 kilometers to the Jewish town of Charax, not far from the city of Tob.
Timothy had been there and gone. He had not done any damage, but he had stationed a very strong force in a nearby fortress.
So Judas gave orders for Dositheus and Sosipater to take some of the Jewish troops and attack the fortress. They were successful and killed more than 10,000 of the soldiers left there by Timothy.

Judas now divided up his soldiers into two groups, placing one under the command of Dositheus and the other under the command of Sosipater. Then they all hurried after Timothy, who had 120,000 soldiers and 2,500 cavalry.

But Timothy learned that Judas' army was coming after him. So he ordered the families of his soldiers to go to the town of Carnaim and take all their baggage with them. This town was a hard place to attack or even to reach because of the narrow passes leading to it.

When the first group of our soldiers reached Timothy's camp, the God who sees everything terrified the enemy troops and sent them scattering in all directions, injuring themselves and others with their own swords.
Our troops eagerly chased Timothy's wicked army and slaughtered almost 30,000 of them.

The soldiers under the command of Dositheus and Sosipater caught up with Timothy himself, who very cleverly said, “Many of your parents and brothers and other relatives are my prisoners, and if you kill me, they will be shown no mercy.”
So after Timothy had solemnly promised to release his prisoners unharmed, he was set free.
Judas and his troops attacked the town of Carnaim and the temple of the goddess Atargatis, where they killed 25,000 people

and destroyed both the temple and the town. Then they surrounded the fortress at Ephron because Lysias and people from many different nations lived there.<sup>[119]</sup> But the people of Ephron had stationed strong young soldiers just outside the town wall, who fiercely defended it. And inside the town they had stored a lot of military supplies and weapons.
comment: [119] because Lysias and … lived there: Some ancient manuscripts have “because all kinds of people lived there.”

text: Our troops prayed for help from our mighty Lord, who crushes powerful enemies. Then we captured Ephron and killed almost 25,000 people.
From Ephron, our army hurried to Scythopolis, a town about 110 kilometers from Jerusalem.
The Jews who lived there told our troops that the people of the town were always kind and helpful, especially in times of trouble.

So our soldiers thanked those people and urged them to always stay on good terms with the Jews. Then Judas and our troops returned to Jerusalem, just before the Harvest Festival, which is also known as Pentecost.
<sup>ⓚ</sup> Following the Harvest Festival, Judas and his troops quickly left Jerusalem and attacked Gorgias, the governor of Idumea,<sup>[120]</sup>
whose army of 3,000 soldiers and 400 cavalry fought back
and killed a few of our troops.

Dositheus, a very strong man, belonged to the group of our cavalry led by Bacenor, and he did something very heroic. He wanted to capture Gorgias alive, so he grabbed that evil man by his coat and started dragging him away. However, a Thracian horseman suddenly rode by Dositheus and chopped off his right arm. Then Gorgias escaped to the town of Marisa.
After our troops under the command of Esdris had been fighting a long time and were worn out, Judas prayed, “Our Lord, please be our leader and help us win this battle.”
In his native language,<sup>[121]</sup> Judas sang some hymns and then shouted the battle cry, as he led his troops in a surprise attack that forced Gorgias and his army to retreat.

Judas brought his troops together and led them to the town of Adullam. It was now the day before the Sabbath, so they went through the traditional ceremonies to prepare themselves for that holy day. Then they celebrated the Sabbath.
The next day, Judas and his troops had to collect the bodies of those who had been killed in battle and to bring them home for burial in their family graves.

<sup>ⓛ</sup> But under the shirt of each dead soldier they found good luck charms in the shape of those idols in the temple at Jamnia. Since our Jewish Law doesn't allow us to wear such things, everyone knew why these soldiers had died in the fighting.
Our troops praised the Lord, who judges fairly and makes all secrets known.
They also begged the Lord to forgive this terrible sin. Judas, that wonderful man, said, “You have seen for yourselves how God punished those who disobeyed him. So I warn you not to sin!”

Then Judas collected from his troops 2,000 silver coins, which he sent to Jerusalem as payment for a sacrifice to forgive this sin. Judas did this generous and honorable thing because he firmly believed God raises the dead to life.
Otherwise, it would have been useless and foolish of him to have spent this money on prayers for the dead.

But he was a man of deep faith, who was convinced that God's faithful servants would receive a wonderful reward after death. So he paid for a special sacrifice to take away the sin of those dead soldiers.
In the year 149<sup>[122]</sup> of the Greek Kingdom, someone told Judas and our troops: King Antiochus Eupator<sup>[123]</sup> is on his way to invade Judea,
comment:
[123] Antiochus Eupator: Antiochus V; see the note at 2.19-23.
[122] year 149: That is, 163 B.C.

text: and he is bringing his guardian Lysias, who runs the government for him. They<sup>[124]</sup> are leading a huge Greek army with 110,000 soldiers, 5,300 cavalry, and 22 elephants. Besides this, they have 300 chariots with sharp blades sticking out from the sides of their wheels.
Menelaus the high priest tried to deceive King Antiochus and Lysias by encouraging them to attack us. He did not do this for the benefit of the country, but to regain his position as high priest.

Meanwhile, Lysias told Antiochus that Menelaus was to blame for all of the country's problems. Then our God, the King of kings, turned Antiochus against Menelaus. And right away, Antiochus sentenced this troublemaker to be killed in the town of Beroea, where they had a special way of executing prisoners.
In Beroea there was a 22 meters tower full of ashes, and the inside wall of the tower sloped down into the ash pile.
Criminals who were guilty of dishonoring a temple or of some other horrible crime were thrown down inside the tower to die.
So that was how the lawbreaker Menelaus died—and without even a proper burial afterwards.
Such a death was a perfect punishment for someone who had so often disgraced the temple altar, together with its holy ashes and fire.
Antiochus was an arrogant and savage king, who wanted to punish the people of Judea more severely than his father had ever done. He was on his way to invade the country,

when Judas found out what was happening. So Judas told the people to pray day and night, and they prayed, “Our Lord, we need you now more than ever before! Please don't let our Law and our nation and our holy temple be destroyed.
You have just given your people a fresh start. Don't let those godless Gentiles rule us again.”

For three days, they lay face down on the ground, crying and refusing to eat, while begging the Lord to have pity and send help. After this, Judas encouraged everyone, then ordered his troops to prepare for battle.
Judas met privately with the nation's leaders, and together they decided that with God's help Judas could attack and defeat Antiochus before he invaded Judea and captured Jerusalem.

So Judas left everything in the hands of God, the Creator of the world, and urged his soldiers to be willing to die for the Law, the temple, Jerusalem, the country, and our Jewish way of life. Judas camped with his army near the town of Modein,

and he told them, “When you go into battle, shout, ‘God gives victory!’ ” Then later that night, he and a chosen group of brave young troops attacked the enemy camp near the king's tent. They killed almost 2,000 foreigners, as well as the soldier who was leading the elephants.<sup>[125]</sup>
comment: [125] as well as … elephants: One possible meaning for the difficult Greek text.

text: Our troops terrified and confused the enemy soldiers, then left victoriously
at dawn, because the Lord had been helping Judas.
King Antiochus had seen how bravely our Jewish soldiers fought. So he decided on a plan to destroy the places where they had stationed their troops.
His troops surrounded and attacked their strong fortress at Beth-Zur, but they were turned back and defeated.
Meanwhile, Judas had been sending supplies to the soldiers in Beth-Zur.
At the same time, a Jewish soldier named Rhodocus was passing secrets to the king, but he was finally captured and put in prison.
Sometime later, Antiochus decided to try a second time to make peace with the people of Beth-Zur. He did so and then attacked Judas. However, he lost this battle as well.

Antiochus had left an official named Philip to run the government for him in Antioch, but Philip rebelled. Antiochus did not know what else to do, and so he worked out an agreement with our people, giving us everything we wanted and promising to treat us fairly. He also offered a sacrifice, then he honored the temple in Jerusalem with gifts,
and he had a friendly meeting with Judas. Finally, Antiochus appointed Hegemonides governor of the territory between the towns of Ptolemais and Gerar.
Then he went to Ptolemais, where the Gentiles were furious with him for making an agreement with us. In fact, they were so angry that they urged him to cancel the treaty.

But Lysias made a speech in which he thoroughly explained the agreement. Everyone was fully convinced and pleased by what he said, and then he left for Antioch. So the invasion by Antiochus turned into a retreat.
Three years later, Judas and his army learned that Demetrius, the son of King Seleucus,<sup>[126]</sup> had sailed into the port city of Tripolis with a powerful army and navy.
comment: [126] Demetrius … Seleucus: Demetrius I ruled 161–150 B.C., and Seleucus IV (ruled 187–175 B.C.). See also the note at 3.3.

text: They also found out that Demetrius had put to death both King Antiochus and Lysias his guardian and was now ruling the country.

A man named Alcimus had earlier been appointed high priest,<sup>[127]</sup> but when our nation was at war,<sup>[128]</sup> he eagerly adopted the Greek way of life. Because of this, Alcimus knew he was in danger from our people and would never be high priest again.
comment:
[128] at war: Some ancient manuscripts have “at peace.”
[127] high priest: Antiochus Eupator (ruled 164–162 B.C.) had made Alcimus the high priest, replacing Menelaus.

text: So in about the year 151<sup>[129]</sup> of the Syrian Kingdom, Alcimus went to King Demetrius and presented him with a gold crown and a palm branch. He also handed him some olive branches from the temple area, as was the custom. However, Alcimus did not mention his desire to be high priest.

Some time later, Demetrius invited Alcimus to a meeting of the royal council and asked him to explain what the Jewish people were planning. Alcimus immediately took this chance to express his own crazy ideas, and he said:
King Demetrius, there is a devout group of Jews,<sup>[130]</sup> who are led by Judas Maccabeus. They are nothing but rebels, and they will never stop causing trouble in your kingdom.
comment: [130] devout group of Jews: The Greek text has “Hasideans,” which translates the Hebrew word “hasidim,” meaning “devout” and refers to Jews who were especially faithful to their religion (see 1 Maccabees 2.42).

text: And so, I have given up the honorable position of high priest that has always been in my family. I have come here,
not only because I am truly concerned about your interests as ruler, but because I am eager to help my people. That foolish group of Jews has brought terrible suffering on our nation.
Now you know the truth, so please be kind and generous, just as you always are, and help our oppressed people.
As long as Judas is alive, your kingdom will never have any peace.
After Alcimus had finished talking, the other advisors told how much they hated Judas. Then Demetrius became so furious
that he immediately appointed Nicanor to be the new governor of Judea. This was the same Nicanor who had been the commander of his war elephants. Then Demetrius sent him to Judea
with orders to kill Judas and scatter his army and afterwards to make Alcimus high priest of the glorious temple.
Many foreigners in Judea had been attacked by Judas at one time or another, and so they rushed to join Nicanor's army, hoping to profit from any trouble they could cause our people.

<sup>ⓜ</sup> When our people found out that Nicanor was coming to attack with all of these Gentiles, they smeared dirt on their heads to show their sorrow. Then they prayed to God, who had chosen them to be his people forever and had always used his power to rescue them.
Judas ordered his troops to march at once to the village of Dessau,<sup>[131]</sup> where they attacked Nicanor.
comment: [131] Dessau: Possibly the same site as Adasa (see 1 Maccabees 7.40,45).

text: Judas' brother Simon also ordered his troops into the battle, but for the moment they were retreating because of a surprise move on the part of Nicanor's army.
Meanwhile, someone told Nicanor just how fearless Judas and his soldiers were, and how fiercely they defended their nation. So Nicanor changed his mind about trying to defeat them in battle,
and instead he sent Posidonius, Theodotus, and Mattathias to make peace with them.
After the details of a peace treaty had been decided, Nicanor<sup>[132]</sup> informed his troops, and they made an agreement.
comment: [132] Nicanor: The Greek has “the leader,” which could also be “Judas.”

text: Then Judas and Nicanor chose a day to meet privately. And when that day arrived, a chariot came out of each camp, and fancy chairs were set up.
Judas had placed armed guards at key positions around the meeting place, just in case the enemy had set a trap. But the meeting was very friendly.
Nicanor stayed in Jerusalem for a time, but he did not cause any trouble, and he sent home many people who had sided with him.
He and Judas became close friends and spent a lot of time together.
Judas even followed Nicanor's advice to get married and start a family like everyone else.

When Alcimus the high priest discovered that Nicanor and Judas were friends, he took a copy of their agreement to King Demetrius<sup>[133]</sup> and said, “Nicanor has betrayed your government. He's going to let that rebel Judas take his place as governor.”
comment: [133] Demetrius: Demetrius I; see the note at 14.1.

text: Demetrius became so irritated and angry as he listened to that worthless Alcimus make these charges that he wrote and told Nicanor, “I do not like the agreement that you made with Judas, and I order you to arrest him and send him to Antioch at once!”
Nicanor was upset and saddened by the orders to cancel an agreement with this innocent man.
Still, he could not disobey the king, so he started looking for an opportunity to take Judas by surprise.
Judas noticed that Nicanor was no longer treating him like a friend, and he guessed that trouble was on the way. So he and a number of his followers went into hiding.
<sup>ⓝ</sup> When Nicanor found out that he had been outsmarted, he went to the famous and holy Jerusalem temple at the time of sacrifice and demanded that the priests hand Judas over to him.
But the priests swore that they did not know where to find Judas.

Nicanor shook his right fist at the temple and said, “Find Judas, or else I swear that I'll destroy this temple and the altar of your God! Then I'll build a glorious temple for the god Dionysus<sup>[134]</sup> on this very spot.”
After this, he left. The priests immediately stretched their arms toward heaven and prayed to God, the Defender of our nation. They said,
<sup>ⓞ</sup> “Our holy Lord God, you have everything, and yet you were pleased to let us build a temple, so that you could live here with us.
We have only recently dedicated this temple again. Please keep it holy forever and ever.”

Razis was one of the most highly respected leaders in Jerusalem, and during the war for freedom, he had risked his life for his faith. In fact, he was so generous that he was known as the father of our country. Someone brought charges against him to Nicanor,
who took this as an opportunity to show his hatred for our people by doing us some real harm. So he sent more than 500 troops to arrest Razis,

who was in a tower surrounded by a walled-in courtyard. But the soldiers started beating down the gate to the courtyard, while shouting orders to set the doors of the tower on fire. Razis knew he was trapped, and he threw himself on his sword,
because he was from an important family and wanted to die with honor, rather than at the hands of godless men.

In all the confusion, Razis only wounded himself with the sword. Meanwhile, crowds of people were forcing their way into the tower. And so, with great courage, Razis climbed to the top of the tower and jumped.
Everyone on the ground quickly moved back, making room for him to land on the ground.
Alive but angry, Razis stood up and ran through the crowd to the top of a steep rock, with blood gushing from his terrible wounds.

He had lost most of his blood, when he tore out his insides with both hands and threw them down at the people, while praying aloud, “Lord of life and breath, I trust you to give these back to me.” Then he died.
Nicanor was told that Judas had led our army to the region of Samaria. So Nicanor planned to attack on the Sabbath, when we would not fight back.<sup>[135]</sup>
comment: [135] Sabbath … not fight back: Many Jews refused to fight on the Sabbath (see 6.11).

text: Nicanor had forced some of our people to join his army, and they said, “The God who sees everything has appointed the Sabbath to be the most holy day, and it would be vicious and cruel to attack Jews on that day.”
But that horrible Nicanor replied, “Did some great ruler in heaven really command you Jews to honor the Sabbath?”
“Yes!” they answered. “And that Ruler is the living Lord and King of Heaven.”
Then Nicanor remarked, “Well, I'm your ruler here on earth, and I order you to get your weapons and finish the job the king gave you to do.” But Nicanor was unable to carry out his cruel plan.
With great pride, Nicanor boasted that he would build a public monument in honor of his victory over Judas and his army.
But Judas was certain that the Lord would come to their rescue,
and he encouraged his troops by saying, “Don't be afraid when the enemy attacks. Remember God All-Powerful will send help from heaven today, just as he has done in the past.”
Judas encouraged his troops by reading to them from their sacred Scriptures and by reminding them of the battles they had already won.
The troops were now excited and eager to fight. So Judas gave them their orders and pointed out that Gentiles never kept their promises.

His words offered them more hope and encouragement than their shields and spears. Judas gave his troops further encouragement by telling them what he had seen in a dream—one<sup>[136]</sup> that he knew they could trust. He said:
comment: [136] seen … one: One possible meaning for the difficult Greek text.

text: I saw Onias the high priest.<sup>[137]</sup> He was both gentle and kind, as well as humble and honest. He also had a gift for speaking and had been brought up well. In my dream, Onias was praying for the whole nation, with his arms outstretched.
comment: [137] Onias the high priest: Menelaus had him murdered around 170 B.C. (see 4.34).

text: Next I saw a dignified and very important looking man with gray hair.
Onias said to me, “This man is God's prophet Jeremiah. He loves our nation and our holy city of Jerusalem so much that he never stops praying for us.”
Then with his right hand, Jeremiah handed me a gold sword and said,
“This sacred sword is a gift from God. Take it and cut your enemies to pieces.”

Everyone, young and old, was encouraged by what Judas had said. They felt so brave and strong that they decided to rush out of camp<sup>[138]</sup> and fight Nicanor's troops in hand-to-hand combat, in order to protect the city, the holy things, and the temple.
comment: [138] to rush out of camp: One possible meaning for the difficult Greek text.

text: In fact, they went into battle so concerned about the sacred temple, that they gave no thought to their own families.
Meanwhile, the people of Jerusalem were anxious and worried about those who had left to fight in the countryside.

Everyone was waiting to see who would win the battle. The enemy troops had lined up and were moving forward, protected on both sides by cavalry. They also had elephants stationed in places where they could help the most.

As Judas watched this huge enemy army advance, he looked carefully at the different kinds of weapons and the savage elephants. Then he stretched his arms toward heaven and prayed to the Lord who works miracles, because he knew that the Lord gives victory to those who deserve it, and not to those who have a lot of swords and armor.
<sup>ⓟ</sup> This is what he prayed: Lord of Heaven, when Hezekiah was king of Judea, you sent an angel who killed 185,000 troops that belonged to King Sennacherib.
Now please send a good angel to make our enemies tremble with fear.
Then use your mighty arm to destroy those who have cursed you and attacked your holy people.
<sup>ⓠ</sup> Nicanor's soldiers blew trumpets and chanted war songs as they attacked.
But our troops begged God for help and fought back
with swords in their hands and prayers in their hearts. They killed at least 35,000 enemy troops that day, and they celebrated because God had shown them his power.
After the battle, Judas and his soldiers were happily on their way home when they found Nicanor lying dead on the ground, but still wearing his armor.
So they all shouted and jumped about, praising the Lord All-Powerful in their native language.<sup>[139]</sup>

Judas had always been a faithful defender of his country, and he was just as patriotic now as he was when he was young. So he ordered his troops to chop off Nicanor's head and right arm and take them to Jerusalem.
When they reached the city, Judas called everyone together. He told the priests to stand in front of the altar, and he sent for the enemy soldiers in the fortress.
Judas showed them the head of that godless Nicanor. Then he let them see the arm of this arrogant and disgusting man, who had shaken his fist at the holy temple of God All-Powerful.

Finally, he cut out the tongue of this worthless man and said, “I am going to feed it piece by piece to the birds. Then I am going to nail his head and arm on the wall of the fortress opposite the temple, as proof of his foolishness.”
Everyone looked toward heaven and prayed, “Our Lord, we praise you for protecting your sacred temple and for showing us your wonderful power.”
Judas nailed Nicanor's head to the wall of the fortress, as evidence that the Lord had helped his people.

<sup>ⓡ</sup> Then everyone decided to remember this day forever by celebrating a festival on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is called Adar in Aramaic.<sup>[140]</sup> The Festival of Mordecai<sup>[141]</sup> is celebrated the day before.
comment:
ⓡ 1 Macc 7.48,49; 3 Macc 6.36.
[140] Aramaic: The Greek has “Syriac,” a later form of Aramaic.
[141] Festival of Mordecai: This is the Festival of Purim that honors Queen Esther and Mordecai for rescuing Jews living in Persia (see Esther 9.20-32).

text: This was how Nicanor died. And now that our people have ruled Jerusalem since his death, it is time to bring my story to an end.
I have tried to write a brief, but interesting book. If it is boring and poorly written, I can only say that I have done my best.

To drink wine by itself can be harmful to your health, and the same can be said of drinking water by itself. But if they are mixed together, they make an enjoyable drink. And so, I have mixed a variety of styles, to make my book interesting both for those who read it aloud and for those who hear it read. The end.
A man named Joakim lived in the city of Babylon
and was married to a very beautiful woman, Susanna the daughter of Hilkiah. Susanna faithfully worshiped the Lord
and obeyed the Law of Moses, just as she had been taught by her parents, who were very religious.
Joakim was very rich and had a large walled garden<sup>[1]</sup> next to his house. He was the most highly honored Jewish man in Babylon, and all the other Jews would come and talk with him.
comment: [1] large walled garden: It seems to have contained a pool of water where Susanna could bathe on warm days (see verses 15-17), several varieties of trees (see verses 53-58), and probably bushes and other plants.

text: One year, two of the older Jewish leaders were appointed to be judges for their community in Babylon. The Lord had said he would punish older leaders who refused to obey his laws and rule the people wisely.<sup>[2]</sup> And that is exactly what these leaders did.
comment: [2] older leaders … wisely: This may be a reference to Jeremiah 29.20-23.

text: The two judges spent so much time at Joakim's house that people went there to have their cases judged.
Each day, the people left the house at noon, then Susanna would go for a walk in her husband's garden.
The two men watched her every day as she walked in the garden, and soon all they could think about was sleeping with her.
They even stopped praying to God and forgot that they were supposed to be fair when they judged legal cases.
Each of them was so ashamed of his desire for her, that they didn't tell the other how they felt.
Day after day they would wait around, hoping to get a look at her.
One day at noon, they said, “It's lunchtime—let's go home.” They left in different directions,

but before long they both turned around and went back to Joakim's house. They saw one another, and each started asking the other why he had come back. Finally, they both admitted they wanted to sleep with Susanna, so they agreed to find a time when they could catch her alone.
The two men watched for their chance, and one hot day, Susanna went into the garden to take a bath. Two of her servant girls were there with her,
though no one else was in the garden, except the two men, who were watching her from their hiding place.
Susanna told her servants, “Bring me some soap and lotion, then close the gates to the garden so I can bathe.”<sup>[3]</sup>
comment: [3] close the gates … bathe: The garden was probably surrounded by high stone walls with solid wood gates, so Susanna thought she would have privacy.

text: The servants did what she said. They shut the main gates to the garden, then they went into the house through the side gate and brought her some soap and lotion. But they did not see the two men.
As soon as the servants had gone, the men left their hiding places. They ran over to Susanna
and said, “Look, the gates are shut, and no one can see us here in the garden. We both want you, and so you had better agree to what we want!
If you refuse, we will testify in court that we saw you send your servant girls away so you could make love with a young man.”
<sup>ⓐ</sup> “I'm trapped, and there's no way out,” Susanna moaned. “If I give in to you, I could be put to death.<sup>[4]</sup> If I refuse, you will have me killed.
comment:
ⓐ Lv 20.10; Dt 22.22.
[4] put to death: If a woman was unfaithful to her husband, she could be put to death (see Deuteronomy 22.22).

text: But it is better to refuse and to suffer what you can do to me, than to sin against God.”
Susanna screamed for help,<sup>[5]</sup> and the two leaders began shouting at her.
comment: [5] screamed for help: Susanna could not be considered innocent if she did not scream for help (see Deuteronomy 22.23,24).

text: One of them ran to the main gates of the garden and opened them.
The household servants heard the noise, and they all rushed in through the side gate to see what had happened to Susanna.
But when they heard the two men accusing her, the servants were ashamed. No one had ever said such things about Susanna before.
The next day, the Jewish people in Babylon came together at Joakim's house. The two men also arrived, ready to go ahead with their terrible plans to have Susanna put to death.
They went to the front of the crowd and said, “Someone bring in Joakim's wife Susanna, the daughter of Hilkiah.”
Susanna came in, along with her parents, her children, and all her relatives.
Susanna was a beautiful woman with a very good figure.
When she came in, her face was covered with a veil. But the two evil men wanted to get one last good look at her, so they ordered her to take off her veil.
Susanna's family was crying, and so was everyone else.
The two men stood in the middle of the group and put their hands on Susanna's head, so they could officially accuse her.<sup>[6]</sup>
comment: [6] put their hands … accuse her: It was a custom for the accusers in a trial to place their hands on the head of the accused (see Leviticus 24.14).

text: But Susanna trusted the Lord to rescue her, and as she cried, she looked up toward heaven.
Then the two men said: While we were walking in the garden, Susanna came in with two servant girls. She shut the gates and told them to leave.
Then a young man came out of hiding and went over to her, and they lay down and started making love.
We were over in the corner of the garden, and we realized they were disobeying God's Law, so we ran over to them.
We saw them making love, but we weren't able to catch the young man, because he was stronger than we were. He opened the gates and ran off.
We grabbed Susanna and asked her who the young man was,
but she refused to tell us. We swear we are telling the truth. Both men were leaders and judges, and so everyone believed them and agreed that Susanna should be put to death.
Susanna cried out, “Eternal God, you know all secrets and everything that will happen in the future.
You know these two men have told evil lies against me in court today. Now I am going to be killed, even though I haven't done anything wrong.”
The Lord heard Susanna's prayer,
and as she was being led away to be executed, he chose a young man named Daniel to help her. Daniel was upset
and shouted, “I will not take part in murdering this woman!”
The crowd turned to him and asked, “What do you mean?”
Daniel went to the center of the crowd and said, “People of Israel, are you fools? You have condemned one of your own women to death, and you haven't even tried to find out what really happened.
Go back to court, and I will prove that the two men who accused Susanna were lying.”
Everyone rushed back to the place where the trial was held, and the group of leaders told Daniel, “So God has chosen you to be a leader, too! Sit down and tell us what you mean.”
Daniel said, “Separate the two men who accused Susanna, and take them far enough away that they can't hear us. Then I will call them over one at a time and question them.”
When the two had been taken to different places, Daniel called the first one over and said: You are an evil old man, and it's clear that you've been sinning for a long time.
<sup>ⓑ</sup> You've been giving unfair decisions in court. You have set the guilty free and condemned innocent people, even though the Lord said not to put an innocent person to death.
Now, you have testified that Susanna was making love with a young man under a tree. So tell us, what kind of a tree was it? “It was a small gum tree,” the man answered.
comment: [7] small gum tree … cut you in half: In Greek, the word for “small gum tree” sounds like the word for “cut in half.”

text: “Is that so?” Daniel replied. “You will pay for that lie with your head! God has already sent his angel to cut you in half.”<sup>[7]</sup>

Daniel ordered the people to take the first man aside and to bring over the second one. Daniel told him: You're not a Jew; you're a filthy Canaanite! You were under the spell of Susanna's beauty, and your desire for her made you do wrong instead of right.
You two men have been frightening women from Israel into sleeping with you. But this faithful Jewish woman wouldn't stand for your evil ways.
Now tell me, when Susanna and this young man were making love, what tree were they under? “They were under a big oak tree,” the man answered.
comment: [8] big oak tree … chop you in half: In Greek, the word for “big oak tree” sounds like the word for “chop in half.”

text: “Is that so?” Daniel replied. “You will pay for that lie with your head! The Lord's angel is waiting to chop you in half,<sup>[8]</sup> and then both of you leaders will be dead.”
The crowd shouted praises to God, because he rescues those who trust him.

<sup>ⓒ</sup> Then they condemned the two leaders, since their answers to Daniel's questions proved they had lied in court to have Susanna killed. The Law of Moses says that anyone who does this should be put to death, and that is what quickly happened to the two men. And so an innocent woman's life was saved.
Susanna's father and mother praised God, and so did her husband Joakim and all her relatives, because she had been found innocent of a shameful crime.
And from then on, Daniel was famous.
When King Astyages was buried in the tomb with his ancestors, Cyrus the Persian took his place as king.<sup>[1]</sup>
comment: [1] King Astyages … king: Astyages was the last king of Media. He was defeated in battle in 550 B.C. by his grandson Cyrus the Great, the king of Persia, who then became king of the Medes and the Persians and ruled until 530 B.C.

text: Daniel was a friend and advisor of King Cyrus, and the king honored him more than anyone else.
<sup>ⓐ</sup> Every day, the Babylonians took food to the idol of their god Bel.<sup>[2]</sup> They brought 272 kilograms of the best wheat flour, 190 liters of wine, and the meat from 40 sheep.
comment:
[2] Bel: Another name for Marduk, the chief god of Babylonia. Bel means “lord.”
ⓐ Is 46.1; Jr 51.44.

text: King Cyrus believed that Bel was a powerful god, and he worshiped the idol every day, but Daniel worshiped only his own God. One day, Cyrus asked Daniel, “Why don't you worship Bel?”
Daniel answered, “I refuse to worship idols—they are made by humans. Instead, I worship the living God, because he created heaven and earth, and he rules everyone who lives.”
“But, Daniel,” the king replied, “isn't Bel a living god? Haven't you seen how much he eats and drinks each day?”
Daniel laughed and said, “Don't be fooled, Your Majesty. That idol is merely clay on the inside and bronze on the outside! It never ate or drank anything.”
This made the king angry. So he called in his priests and told them, “Prove to me that Bel<sup>[3]</sup> is eating all this food! If you can't, then you will die.
comment: [3] Prove to me that Bel: Greek “Tell me who.”

text: But if you can prove that Bel really is eating the food, then Daniel will die, because he has insulted the god Bel.” Daniel said, “Your Majesty, that sounds fair enough to me.”
Now there were 70 priests of Bel, and they and their wives had lots of children. The king went with Daniel into the temple of Bel,

and the priests said, “Your Majesty, we will go outside now. Please set out the food and the wine yourself, then shut the door. Drip some hot wax along the edge of the door and press your ring into the wax to leave your special mark. This will show that only you are allowed to open the door.<sup>[4]</sup>
comment: [4] Drip some hot wax … open the door: The kings ring had a special design on it, and he pressed the ring into the soft, hot wax. Then, after the wax cooled, the door could not be opened without breaking the wax.

text: When you come back in the morning, if you find that Bel hasn't eaten everything, then you can put us to death. But if the food is gone, this will prove Daniel has been lying, and you can put him to death.”
The priests were not worried at all. They had a secret trap door under the table, and that was how they sneaked into the temple every night to eat the food.

The priests left, and the king arranged Bel's food on the table. Then Daniel told his servants to scatter ashes over the temple floor. The king was the only other person who saw them do this. They shut the door as they went outside, and the king placed his special mark on some hot wax along the edge of the door so that they could tell if the door had been opened. Then they all left.
Later that night, the priests and their wives and children went to the temple as they always did, and they ate and drank everything.
Early the next morning, the king brought Daniel to the temple
and asked him, “Daniel, has the wax been broken? Has the door been opened?” “No, Your Majesty,” Daniel answered.
As soon as the door was opened,<sup>[5]</sup> the king looked at the empty table and shouted, “Bel, you are a great god, and you always tell the truth!”
Daniel just laughed. He kept the king from entering the temple and said, “Look at the floor—I wonder who left all those footprints?”
The king said, “I can see the footprints of men, women, and children!”

He was furious and told his guards to arrest the priests along with their wives and children. Then the priests showed him the secret door they used when they sneaked into the temple to eat the food that was on Bel's table.
The king told his guards to kill the priests and their families. Then he gave the temple and the idol of Bel to Daniel, who had them destroyed.
The Babylonians also worshiped a huge dragon<sup>[6]</sup> as a god,
comment: [6] dragon: Or “snake”; the Greek word can refer either to a snake or to an imaginary snake-like monster. The snake may have represented the Babylonian goddess Tiamat.

text: and the king of Babylonia said to Daniel, “You can't say this god isn't alive! So you ought to worship it.”
Daniel answered, “I worship the Lord, because he is the living God.
Your Majesty, if you will give me permission, I will kill this dragon, without striking it with a sword or a club.” “I give you permission to try,” the king replied.

Daniel put some tar and animal fat and hair in a pot and boiled them together. Then he shaped the mixture into cakes that looked something like loaves of barley bread and fed them to the dragon. It swelled up and burst open, and Daniel said, “Take a look at what you Babylonians worship.”

But when the Babylonians heard what had happened, they were so upset with the king that they began plotting against him. “Has the king become a Jew?” they asked each other. “First he destroyed our idol Bel and killed its priests. And now he has killed our dragon-god.”
The Babylonians went to the king and said, “Hand Daniel over to us. If you don't, we will kill you and everyone in your family!”
The king saw that he really had no choice, and so he was forced to let them have Daniel.

<sup>ⓑ</sup> The Babylonians kept seven lions in a large pit and fed them two people and two sheep each day. Daniel was thrown into this pit, and for the next six days the lions were given no other food. The Babylonians wanted to make sure the lions would eat Daniel.
Meanwhile, far away in Judea, the prophet Habakkuk had made a pot of stew and put some pieces of bread into a bowl. He was about to take it to the workers who were harvesting wheat in the fields,
when an angel told him, “Take this meal to the lion pit in Babylon, and give it to Daniel.”
Habakkuk replied, “But, sir, I've never been to Babylon, and I don't know where the lion pit is.”
<sup>ⓒ</sup> The angel lifted up Habakkuk by his hair and carried him to Babylon as fast as the wind. He set Habakkuk down at the edge of the lion pit,
and Habakkuk shouted, “Daniel, take this food God has sent you.”
Daniel prayed, “Thank you, God, for remembering me. You always take care of those who love you.”
Daniel got up and ate the food, while God's angel quickly returned Habakkuk to his home.
Seven days later, the king came to the lion pit to mourn for Daniel. But when he looked into the pit, he saw Daniel sitting there, alive.
Then the king shouted out this prayer: “You, the Lord God of Daniel, are powerful! You alone are the true God!”
The king ordered Daniel to be pulled up out of the pit, then he arrested the men who had tried to have Daniel killed. The king had them thrown into the pit, and he watched the lions gobble them up.

<sup>[1]</sup> [2-4] <sup>ⓐ</sup> Mordecai son of Jair<sup>[2]</sup> was a Jew from the Benjamin tribe, and he lived in the city of Susa in Persia. Mordecai had been taken away from Jerusalem as a prisoner, when King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylonia<sup>[3]</sup> had captured King Jehoiachin.<sup>[4]</sup> Mordecai had become an important official in the court of Artaxerxes the Great,<sup>[5]</sup> the king of Persia. And on the first day of the month of Nisan<sup>[6]</sup> in the second year that Artaxerxes was king, Mordecai had a dream. In Mordecai's dream,
comment:
ⓐ 2 K 24.10-16.
[11] Susa: A city east of Babylon and a winter home for Persian kings.
[10] King Artaxerxes: King Artaxerxes: See the note on Artaxerxes the Great at 11.2-4.
[7] That night: Or “One night.”
[1] The verses 11.2—12.6 are sometimes numbered as A.1-17 or 1.1a-1s.

text: [5] there was confusion and unrest all over the world. He heard crashing thunder, and the earth shook with an earthquake
[6] as two huge dragons went toward each other, ready to fight. They roared,
comment:
[8] position: Or “a higher position.”
[12] festival: Most Greek manuscripts “wedding party”; some Greek manuscripts “drinking party.”

text: [7] and every nation on earth prepared to go to war against God's people.
comment: [9] Haman son of Hammedatha: The Greek text adds “a Bougean.” However, the meaning of this term is not known.

text: [8] It was a dark and hopeless time; the world was full of suffering and hardship and conflict.
[9] God's people were afraid of the disaster that was about to strike them, and they were sure they were going to be killed.
[10] But when they cried out to God for help, a tiny stream suddenly became a mighty river,
comment: [13] Vashti: The Hebrew form of the name; Greek “Astin.”

text: [11] and the sun rose and shone brightly. God's people were given power, and they destroyed those who had oppressed them.
comment: [14] Haman: This was probably a different Haman than Haman son of Hammedatha mentioned elsewhere in the book.

text: [12] Mordecai woke up, but he knew that in his dream he had seen what God was planning to do. And so, Mordecai thought about his dream all day, trying to understand exactly what it meant.
[1] That night,<sup>[7]</sup> Mordecai was in the palace courtyard. He was resting not far from Gabatha and Tharra, the two officers who were on guard duty.
[2] Mordecai overheard them talking, and as he listened carefully, he realized they were planning to murder King Artaxerxes. Mordecai warned Artaxerxes about the plot to kill him.
comment: [15] friends: Probably refers to an important group known as “The Friends of the King,” the kings most honored and close advisors.

text: [3] The two officers confessed when Artaxerxes questioned them, and so he gave orders for them to be put to death.
[4] He also ordered that a report of these events be written in his records, and Mordecai also wrote down what had happened.
[5] Artaxerxes appointed Mordecai to a position<sup>[8]</sup> in the royal court and gave him a reward.

[6] Haman son of Hammedatha<sup>[9]</sup> was one of the king's most honored officials, and he became angry because the two officers had been put to death. So he decided to find a way to harm Mordecai and all the Jewish people.

[1-3] <sup>ⓑ</sup> King Artaxerxes<sup>[10]</sup> lived in his capital city of Susa<sup>[11]</sup> and ruled 127 provinces from India to Ethiopia. During the third year of his rule, King Artaxerxes paid for a festival and asked a special group known as the Friends of the King to come. He also invited a large number of people from his own empire and from other nations. The rulers of the Persian provinces came, and so did many important people from the province of Media.
[4] For 180 days Artaxerxes showed off his wealth and spent a lot of money to impress his guests with the celebrations.
[5] After this festival,<sup>[12]</sup> Artaxerxes invited all the men in the city of Susa to a drinking party in the courtyard of his palace. The party went on for six days.

[6] The palace had been decorated with cotton and linen curtains tied back with purple linen cords. These cords were attached to gold and silver square pegs on columns, which were made of marble and other stones. Couches of gold and silver were arranged on pavement that had all kinds of designs made from emeralds, mother-of-pearl, and marble. These couches were covered with see-through cloth woven with designs of different colors, and around each couch were roses.

[7] The wine cups were made of gold and silver, and the king had put on display one small cup that was decorated with rubies worth over 1,000 tons of silver. There was plenty of the king's favorite sweet wine,
[8] and he had told everyone, “Drink all you want!” Then he told his servants, “Keep our cups full.”
[9] Meanwhile, in another part of the palace, Queen Vashti<sup>[13]</sup> was giving a drinking party for the women of Susa.
[10] By the seventh day of the party, King Artaxerxes was really feeling happy, and he told his seven personal servants Haman,<sup>[14]</sup> Bazan, Tharra, Boraze, Zatholtha, Abataza, and Tharaba

[11] to bring Vashti to him. Artaxerxes wanted to place the crown on her head again, to show everyone she was the queen. He also wanted to show his governors and the people from different countries just how beautiful she really was.
[12] But Vashti did not go back with the servants—she refused to obey the king! Artaxerxes was furious because she had embarrassed him,
[13] and he said to his friends,<sup>[15]</sup> “Vashti has refused to obey me! Tell me what the law says about a case like this.”

[14] Arkesaeus, Sarsathaeus, and Malesear went up to the king. They were his highest officials as well as being governors of the Persians and Medes, and they were always given the seats closest to the king.
[15] They said, “You sent your servants with a command for Queen Vashti. But since she refused to obey you, the law says she must be punished.”

[16-17] Then Muchaeus, another official, told the king and the governors: King Artaxerxes has told us what Queen Vashti said and how she refused to obey him. She humiliated the king, and soon all his governors and officials will be humiliated too.
[18] We are governors of the Persians and Medes, but when our wives hear what the queen said to the king, our wives will dare to insult us in the same way.

[19] Your Majesty, if you agree, you should make a law that Vashti is never to be with you again. Put it in writing, according to the laws of the Medes and Persians, so that it cannot be changed. And find some other woman who is more suited to be queen than Vashti.
[20] Finally, make sure everyone in your kingdom is told what you have decided to do. Then each wife will honor her husband, whether he is rich or poor.
[21] Artaxerxes and his officials liked what Muchaeus had said,

[22] and Artaxerxes sent a copy of the law to all of his provinces. Each copy was written in the language of the province to which it was sent, and it said that every husband must be respected by his family.
After a while, King Artaxerxes got over being angry. He stopped being lonely for Vashti, and he forgot about all the things he had said about her when he divorced her.
Then his personal servants said: Your Majesty, a search must be made to find you some beautiful young women who have good reputations

and are virgins. You can select officers in every province to bring them to the place where you keep your wives here in the capital city of Susa. Your servant who is in charge of your wives can be in charge of the young women and make sure they are given beauty creams and whatever else they need.
Choose the woman who pleases you the most and make her your queen instead of Vashti. Artaxerxes liked these suggestions, and he followed them.
At this time a Jew named Mordecai<sup>[16]</sup> was living in Susa, the capital of Persia. His father was named Jair, and his grandfather Shimei was the son of Kish from the tribe of Benjamin.
<sup>ⓒ</sup> Mordecai<sup>[17]</sup> was one of the people that King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylonia<sup>[18]</sup> had taken prisoner from Jerusalem.
comment:
ⓒ 2 K 24.10-16; 2 Ch 36.10.
[17] Mordecai: Or “Kish”; Greek “He.”
[18] King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylonia: Ruled 605–562 B.C.

text: Mordecai's uncle Aminadab had a daughter named Esther. But Aminadab and his wife had died, and so Mordecai had raised his cousin Esther as his own daughter. She had grown into a beautiful young woman,

and when the king's command was sent out, she was taken to the palace along with the many young women who had been brought to Susa. She and the others were placed in the care of Gai, who was in charge of all the king's wives.

Esther was Gai's favorite, and he began her beauty treatments at once. He also gave her plenty of food and seven maids from the king's palace. Esther and her servants were treated better than the other women.
Mordecai had warned Esther not to tell anyone she was a Jew, and she obeyed him.
He was anxious to find out what would happen to her. So each day he would walk back and forth in front of the courtyard at the building where the women lived.

Each of the young women was given beauty treatments for a whole year before going to King Artaxerxes. The first six months her skin was rubbed with olive oil and myrrh, and the last six months it was treated with beauty cream mixed with spices.
Then she spent one night alone with Artaxerxes. He sent a servant to bring her to the palace

in the evening. The next morning she went to the place where the king's wives stayed after being with him. There the king's servant Gai was in charge of them, and only the ones that the king asked for by name could go back to him.

Esther's turn<sup>[19]</sup> to go to King Artaxerxes came in the month of Adar, the twelfth month,<sup>[20]</sup> in the seventh year that he was king. Esther did everything Gai told her to do. Everyone liked her,
comment:
[19] Esthers turn: Greek “the turn of Esther, the daughter of Aminadab the brother of Mordecais father” (see also 2.7).
[20] the month of Adar, the twelfth month: From about mid-February to mid-March.

text: and even Artaxerxes liked her better than any of the other young women he had seen. In fact, he fell in love with her and placed the queen's crown on her head.
Then he gave a seven-day drinking party to celebrate his marriage to Esther, and he made a law that for a certain length of time, no one in his kingdom would have to pay any taxes.
At this time, Mordecai was serving as one of the king's officials.

He had warned Esther not to tell anyone that she was a Jew, but he had also told her to continue worshiping God and obeying his commands, just as she had done when she was living in Mordecai's home. Esther obeyed Mordecai and did not change her way of life.
The king's two chief bodyguards were angry that Mordecai had been promoted, and they decided to murder the king.
But when Mordecai found out about their plot, he warned Esther, and she told the king.

King Artaxerxes questioned the two men to make sure they were guilty, then he had them hanged. He also had someone write up a report praising Mordecai for the kindness he had shown, and the report was placed in the royal library.
Later, King Artaxerxes promoted Haman the son of Hammedatha<sup>[21]</sup> to the highest position in his kingdom.
comment:
[27] The verses 13.1-7 are sometimes numbered as B.1-7 or as 3.13a-13g.
[21] Haman the son of Hammedatha: The Greek text adds “a Bougean.” However, the meaning of this term is not known.

text: The king ordered all of his officials to bow down to Haman, and all of them obeyed except Mordecai.
The other officials went to Mordecai and asked, “Why are you ignoring what the king said?”

They spoke to Mordecai like this for several days, but he told them he was a Jew and would not bow down to Haman. The other officials went to Haman and told him that Mordecai was Jewish and refused to do what the king said.
Haman was furious when he learned that Mordecai refused to bow down to him,
and he started planning how to get rid of all the Jews in the kingdom.

It was now the twelfth year that Artaxerxes was king, and Haman decided<sup>[22]</sup> to find out what would be the best month and day to kill Mordecai and the rest of the Jews. He found that the best date was Adar<sup>[23]</sup> fourteenth.
comment:
[22] decided: The Greek text has “cast lots,” which were small pieces of wood or bone that were often used to get an answer from a god. They were tossed on the ground, and the way they landed showed what the answer was.
[23] Adar: See the note at 2.15,16.

text: Then Haman went to King Artaxerxes and said, “Your Majesty, the people from a certain nation are scattered throughout your kingdom. Their customs are different from ours, and they refuse to obey your laws. You would be better off to get rid of them.
If you give orders for all of them to be killed, I will pay over 340 tons of silver to your treasury.”<sup>[24]</sup>
comment: [24] I will pay … to your treasury: Possibly from the possessions of the Jews that would be killed.

text: Artaxerxes handed his royal ring to Haman, so the law against the Jews could be made official.<sup>[25]</sup>
comment: [25] ring … official: Melted wax was used to seal a document, and while the wax was still soft, the kings ring was pressed into it. The special design left in the wax showed that the document was official.

text: Then the king said, “Do what you want with those people! And you can keep their money.”

On the thirteenth day of the first month,<sup>[26]</sup> Haman called in the king's secretaries and ordered them to write a letter and make copies in every language used in the kingdom. The letter was to be written in the name of King Artaxerxes and sent to the generals of his army and to the governors of his 127 provinces from India to Ethiopia.
comment: [26] the first month: Nisan (also called Abib), the first month of the Hebrew calendar, from about mid-March to mid-April.

text: Then messengers would deliver the copies of the letter, which said that on a certain day in Adar, the twelfth month, the people were to get rid of all the Jews and take their property. <sup>[27]</sup>
[1] This is a copy of the letter: From Artaxerxes, the Great King, to the governors and officials of my 127 provinces from India to Ethiopia.

[2] I rule many nations, and I am the most powerful king in the world. But I have never used my power in a proud or arrogant way. Instead, I have always been reasonable and kind to the people in my kingdom. I know they want peace, and so I have decided to make every part of my kingdom peaceful and safe for travel.

[3-4] <sup>ⓓ</sup> When I asked my advisors to tell me the best way to bring about peace and safety, Haman had an answer. He is the wisest man in my kingdom and is always loyal and kind, which is why I made him my highest official. He told us that the people from a certain nation are scattered throughout all the other nations of the world. These people are always causing trouble, and they have laws that make them disobey those of the nations where they live. And when I make laws in the hope of uniting the people in my kingdom, the people of this nation refuse to obey.

[5] In fact, they seem to be the only people who always go against everyone else and insist on following their own strange customs. They don't like the way I rule, and they commit every horrible crime they can to keep my kingdom from being peaceful.

[6] Haman, my highest and most honored official, has written letters telling what these people are like. So I have made a law that all of them—even the women and children—must be put to death without mercy on the fourteenth day of the month of Adar<sup>[28]</sup> of this year.

[7] They have worked against us for a long time, and so on this one day, we will use violence to send them down to the world of the dead. Then our kingdom will be peaceful and free from trouble forever.
[14] Copies of this letter were displayed publicly in each province, so that every nation would be ready for that day.
[15] Copies were quickly posted in Susa, but no one in the city could figure out what was going on. Meanwhile, Artaxerxes and Haman got drunk together.

Mordecai learned what had happened, and he tore his clothes in sorrow and put on clothes made of sackcloth.<sup>[29]</sup> Then he sprinkled himself with ashes<sup>[30]</sup> and ran through the city streets, shouting at the top of his voice, “An innocent nation is going to be destroyed!”
comment:
[29] sackcloth: A rough, dark-colored cloth made from goat or camel hair and used to make grain sacks. It was worn in times of trouble or sorrow.
[30] sprinkled … ashes: A way of showing sorrow.

text: But he could go only as far as the palace gate, because no one wearing sackcloth or sprinkled with ashes was allowed inside the palace courtyard.
In every province, wherever the king's orders had been read, the Jews cried bitterly and mourned; they put on sackcloth and sprinkled themselves with ashes.
When Esther's servant girls and her other servants told her what Mordecai was doing, she was terribly upset and sent Mordecai some clothes to wear instead of the sackcloth. But he refused.
Then Esther called in her personal servant Hachratheus and sent him to find out exactly what was the matter with Mordecai.<sup>[31]</sup>
comment: [31] Mordecai: Some manuscripts add “Hachratheus went to Mordecai, who was in the street across from the city gate.”

text: Mordecai told Hachratheus everything that had happened, and especially how Haman had promised to put over 340 tons of silver into the king's treasury if all the Jews were killed.

Mordecai handed Hachratheus a copy of the orders posted in Susa for the murder of the Jews, then he said: Hachratheus, after you show these orders to Esther and explain what they mean, ask her to go to the king and beg him to have pity on her people, the Jews! Then give her this message from me: “Esther, remember that I raised you and that you were once an ordinary person just as we are. And now Haman, the king's highest official, has lied about us, and we have been condemned to die. Beg the Lord for help, then speak to the king for us and save us from death.”
comment: [34] The verses 13.8—14.19 are sometimes numbered as C.1-30 or 4.17a-17z.

text: Hachratheus went back to Esther and told her what Mordecai had said.
Esther answered, “Tell Mordecai

that there is a law about going into the inner courtyard to see the king. Everyone in the kingdom knows that if you go in without being invited by him, the penalty is death. The only thing that can save you is for him to hold out his golden scepter<sup>[32]</sup> to you. And it's been 30 days since he has asked for me.”
comment:
[37] power: Greek “scepter,” a decorated rod, often made of gold, that a king held in his hand as a sign of his royal power.
[32] scepter: A decorated rod, often made of gold, that a king held in his hand as a sign of his royal power.

text: When Hachratheus told Mordecai everything Esther had said,
Mordecai told him to go back to Esther and say, “Esther, if all the Jews are going to be killed, don't think that you will escape.
If you refuse to help us, we will find help and protection from someone else, but you and your family will be wiped out. It could be that you were made queen just for a time like this!”
Esther sent Hachratheus<sup>[33]</sup> back to Mordecai to tell him,

“Hurry and bring together all the Jews in Susa. Tell them to go without eating for my sake. Don't eat or drink for three days and nights, and my servant girls and I will do the same. Then I will break the law and go in to see the king, even if it means I must die!”
Mordecai left and did everything Esther had told him to do.
<sup>[34]</sup> [8] <sup>ⓔ</sup> Mordecai prayed and begged the Lord to save his people, and he thanked the Lord for the times he had helped them in the past.
[9] Mordecai said: Our Lord, you are King and Ruler of the whole earth, and so no one can stop you when you decide to save Israel.
[10] You are the Creator of heaven and earth and of all the amazing things on earth as well.
[11] Everything obeys your commands, and no one can stand against you.
[12] Since you know everything, you know that I wasn't being proud or arrogant or vain when I have refused to bow down to that arrogant Haman.
[13] I would even kiss the soles of his feet if that would save Israel.
[14] But you are my God, and that's why I refused to honor a human the way I honor you. I don't want to sound arrogant, but I won't bow down to anyone except you.

[15-16] <sup>ⓕ</sup> Long ago, our ancestor Abraham worshiped you, Lord. You are our God and king, and we are your people. We have always belonged to you, ever since you set us free from Egypt. Don't abandon us now; save us from our enemies, who want to destroy us.
[17] Answer my prayer and have mercy on us. Turn our sadness into celebration. Let us live, and we will sing praises to your name; we honor you, so please don't let death silence our voices.
[18] All the Israelites wept bitterly, because they could see they were going to die.
[1] Queen Esther was worried and upset, and she realized that only the Lord could save her people from being killed.

[2] So she took off her beautiful royal robes and put on clothes that showed it was a time of suffering and death. She put ashes and dirt<sup>[35]</sup> all over her head, rather than using any of her expensive lotions.<sup>[36]</sup> And instead of doing everything she could to look beautiful and dignified, Esther just let her long hair hang down in tangles.
[3] Then she prayed to the Lord God of Israel: You, Lord, are the only King we have. And no one except you can help me now, because I'm all alone,
[4] and I've decided to risk my life.

[5] Ever since I was born, those who belong to my family's tribe have told me that long ago you chose our ancestors to become Israel, your own special people. You have always kept your promises to us.
[6] But we sinned against you, Lord, and you let our enemies conquer us
[7] because we had worshiped their gods. You were right to punish us this way.
[8] But our enemies weren't satisfied just to keep us in bitter slavery. Now they have made an agreement with their idols

[9] to kill all of us, your special people. And if they get rid of us, your promises to us will be meaningless. We will no longer be able to praise you, and we won't be able to worship you and offer sacrifices in your temple.
[10] Then the nations will praise their idols and forever give honor to a mere earthly king.

[11] Please, Lord, don't hand over your royal power<sup>[37]</sup> to gods that are nothing. We have fallen down, but don't let our enemies laugh at us. They have made plans to kill us, but turn their own plans against them. And make an example of the one who is behind those plans.
[12] You are king of the gods and are above every other ruler, so show your power and rescue us in this time of great danger. Give me courage

[13] and the right words to say to the king,<sup>[38]</sup> so that he will change his mind and hate the man who is attacking us. I pray that the king will get rid of him and those who support his plot.
[14] <sup>ⓖ</sup> Reach down and save us, Lord. I'm all alone—no one but you can help me now.

[15-16] You know all things—you know how much I hate being the queen of this evil country. I hate the honor that the people give me, and wearing my crown when I go out in public is the same as wearing a blood-soaked rag placed around my head. That's why I refuse to wear it in my own living quarters. And you also know that I even hate to sleep with my husband the king, because he isn't one of your people and isn't circumcised.
[17] I am your servant, Lord, and I have never eaten at the same table as Haman, and I have never attended the king's banquets or drunk wine that had been offered to other gods.
[18] You are the Lord God that Abraham worshiped, and only you have given me any joy since I was brought here.
[19] We have little hope left. But you, Lord, have power over everything, so please hear our prayers and rescue us from those who are evil. And help me not to be afraid.
<sup>[39]</sup> Esther prayed for three days,<sup>[40]</sup> then she changed her clothes and put on her royal robes once again.<sup>[41]</sup>
comment:
[40] three days: See Add C 4.16.
[39] The verses 15.1-16 are sometimes numbered as D.1-16 or 5.1a-1f, 2, 2a, 2b, 15.4-19. Addition D replaces 5.1,2 of the Hebrew text.
[41] once again: See 14.2.

text: When Esther finished getting ready, she was beautiful. She prayed once more to God, the Savior who watches over all things, and she left with her two favorite servant girls.
One of them helped her walk,
and the other followed right behind and kept her long robes from dragging on the floor.
Esther's beauty was perfect. Her face was glowing with happiness, as though she knew the king loved her. However, in her heart she felt paralyzed by fear.

Finally Esther passed through the last doorway and into the throne room, where she stopped in front of King Artaxerxes. He was seated there, wearing majestic royal robes that were covered with jewels and gold—a terrifying sight.
The king looked up, and his face was burning with royal anger. Queen Esther went pale! She fainted and fell right on top of her servant,<sup>[42]</sup> who was just in front of her.
comment: [42] right on top of her servant: One possible meaning for the difficult Greek text.

text: Then God changed the king's anger into concern for Esther, and the king jumped up and ran over to her. He took Esther in his arms, holding her until she came to. Then he comforted her and gently said,
